transcript:
Meeting: Spectra AI x Redwood — Reserved node commitment & chaos planning
Date: 2026-08-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (AE), Ethan Brooks (SE), Liam Ortiz (CTO), Priya Nair (Head of ML), Jonas Petrov (Infra), Sara Kim (Product)

Summary: quick intake to validate sizing and security constraints; heavy on operational scenarios (chaos/failover) and cost/latency tradeoffs.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Ethan, our solutions engineer. quick roll call?
[00:06] Liam Ortiz: yeah this is Liam, CTO at Spectra. hey.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Priya here, head of ML.
[00:10] Jonas Petrov: Jonas, infra. we'll be the ones setting up VPCs and peering.
[00:14] Ethan Brooks: great, thanks. quick agenda — sizing/commit tiers, isolation/tenancy, burst and warm pool behavior, then security and next steps. sound ok?
[00:21] Sara Kim: yep fine.
[00:24] Maya Chen: perfect. Liam can you start with current stack and why you're thinking dedicated?
[00:29] Liam Ortiz: sure. we run inference for multi-turn dialogue, about 200 reqs/s peak across customers, p99 tail is what kills us. currently self-hosted on GCP, running mixed workloads, we're seeing noisy neighbor spikes, cost is creeping. long story short we want predictable latency and to avoid building orchestration ourselves.
[00:45] Maya Chen: got it. and target SLO?
[00:48] Priya Nair: p95 under 150ms, p99 under 400ms for short prompts (<512 tokens). for longer prompts the tolerance is higher but we want predictability.
[00:58] Ethan Brooks: are you planning a full migration to Dedicated or hybrid — some traffic to Redwood hosted for burst?
[01:04] Liam Ortiz: preference is Dedicated for steady state, but we'd like Redwood hosted as overflow for spikes — only if we can guarantee data handling rules.
[01:12] Jonas Petrov: also need VPC peering and KMS in our account, can't have keys stored external.
[01:18] Maya Chen: okay that maps to our Dedicated+burst pattern; we support VPC peering and we have a private KMS integration option so keys can be customer-managed, we can pull SOC2 docs. Ethan, maybe talk tech?
[01:26] Ethan Brooks: sure. so our Dedicated offering gives you reserved GPU pools — you can choose a commit for N nodes, those are tenant-isolated by default at the runtime layer. we do node fencing: noisy tenant gets quarantined to a hot standby and we fallback to a separate pool. for burst we offer warm-pools that keep model weights and KV cache warmed. the tradeoff is cost: warm-pools are reserved compute, so they're part of the commit or you can pay a smaller hourly for ephemeral warmers.
[01:48] Priya Nair: how quick to scale to 2x? our traffic has sudden surges, like a few minutes to ramp.
[01:54] Ethan Brooks: varies on model size and KV cache; for an Llama-like 30B model on 8xA100 topology we'd see prewarm to steady within ~45-90s if weights are cold, but with warm-pool reuse you can be sub-10s for first token. that's where KV cache reuse helps a lot.
[02:10] Jonas Petrov: you said node fencing, can you clarify what that means operationally? is it hypervisor level?
[02:15] Ethan Brooks: good question. it's a combination: we fence at the runtime layer, isolate the process, and then evict the tenant from the shared scheduler. not hypervisor-level by default in Dedicated — it's isolated GPUs, but the runtime keeps tenants logical separation. you can opt for dedicated physical nodes per tenant (single-tenant nodes) if you need full blast radius elimination.
[02:33] Liam Ortiz: ok so single-tenant nodes cost what relative? ballpark?
[02:36] Maya Chen: single-tenant nodes are roughly 1.7-2x the price of multi-tenant reserved nodes because of lower utilization; we'll send precise tiers.
[02:44] Sara Kim: what's the experience when a canary causes high memory thrash — rollback options?
[02:49] Ethan Brooks: we support canary rollouts with autoswitch fallback; if the canary exceeds thresholds we automatically switch traffic to previous model and isolate the node. plumbed into the console with alerts and tracing.
[03:00] Priya Nair: we have strict region requirements for KMS — keys must remain in eu-west-1. can you support that?
[03:05] Maya Chen: yes, we have KMS integrations that keep keys in customer account regionally. we'll note region requirements and document that.
[03:11] Liam Ortiz: what's the audit log retention — we need 1 year for forensic?
[03:15] Maya Chen: standard retention is 90 days but enterprise add-on supports 1 year and we can export to customer S3 for long-term retention.
[03:22] Jonas Petrov: about burst: you mentioned using Redwood hosted as overflow; what's the data handling model there — do we risk data leaving our VPC?
[03:30] Ethan Brooks: hosted overflow goes through our hosted API; we offer an encryption-in-transit and at-rest model, but it won't be under your VPC or KMS unless you choose Private deployment. for sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated with an explicit warm pool and pre-provisioned overflow contracts, or Private deployment for full VPC control.
[03:47] Liam Ortiz: might want a hybrid — steady on Dedicated with warm-pool and a hard cap that fails open to lowest-privilege hosted if overflow, but filter to scrub PII. is that feasible?
[03:58] Maya Chen: yes, we can implement content filters and redaction on overflow and a routing policy to control which endpoints can overflow. good pattern for regulated customers.
[04:07] Priya Nair: can you explain how KV cache is persisted across restarts — in our tests we saw cache warm-up cost hit p99 badly.
[04:14] Ethan Brooks: KV cache is persisted to local NVMe on the node and across warm-pool handoffs we transfer cache chunks to minimize recompute. there are size limits; extremely long contexts will still cause cold starts. our optimize tool can recommend quantization and batch sizing to reduce that impact.
[04:30] Sara Kim: any pitfalls we should plan for in first 30 days?
[04:33] Ethan Brooks: common things: mismatch in QPS patterns, under-provisioning of warm-pool for burst, and not pinning critical endpoints to single-tenant nodes. we usually run a short load-finding stage to tune batch sizes and prewarm counts.
[04:45] Maya Chen: ok let's talk pricing tradeoffs quickly — commit bigger pools lowers per-token costs but raises capital. smaller commit plus higher burst rates to hosted increases network and egress considerations.
[04:56] Liam Ortiz: high level we want predictable monthly cost but also confidence during marketing spikes. find a middle ground.
[05:02] Ethan Brooks: one approach: commit to baseline for steady traffic, keep a modest warmpool sized for most spikes, and buy a burst overlay contract with pre-negotiated hosted rates. that buys predictability.
[05:12] Jonas Petrov: one constraint — our infra team can't accept outbound peering to third party unless there's a transit VPC and strict route controls. can Redwood peer with a transit VPC?
[05:21] Maya Chen: yes, we support peering via transit and Private deployments can be placed in your account with direct connectivity, we can map that out in the security deep-dive.
[05:28] Liam Ortiz: how do you handle upgrades to runtime that might change latency characteristics? we need regressions prevented.
[05:34] Ethan Brooks: we have rollouts with canaries and performance regression tests. Redwood Optimize will detect changes tied to prompt sets and alert; you can pin model/runtime versions per route to avoid surprises.
[05:46] Priya Nair: curious about observability — token-level breakdowns? traces?
[05:50] Ethan Brooks: yep token-level cost/latency breakdown per request, per-model dashboard, and exported traces to your APM. we can also add custom tracing hooks to tag requests.
[05:59] Sara Kim: ok, practical ask — can we run a bench next week? we want to show our real prompt mix and measure tail.
[06:03] Maya Chen: absolutely. Ethan will own the harness and we'll coordinate.
[06:06] Ethan Brooks: i'll provision a 4-node 8xA100 test pool and a warm-pool overlay and run a couple 2-hour runs with your prompt set. i'll share results and tuned batch settings.
[06:15] Liam Ortiz: excellent. last one — failure mode: if Dedicated pool is hit and warm pool exhausted, do you throttle or fail open to hosted?
[06:23] Ethan Brooks: configurable: throttle (queue) or failover to hosted. we can hard-fail for safety critical flows or allow degraded quality hosted fallback. we'll model both in bench runs.
[06:33] Maya Chen: ok i think that's most of it. quick recap and owners — we'll send pricing tiers, SE bench, and schedule security deep-dive. any other final issues?
[06:42] Priya Nair: just to reiterate — we need KMS in eu-west-1 and audit retention to meet compliance.
[06:47] Maya Chen: noted. Jonas?
[06:49] Jonas Petrov: i'll confirm network constraints and share a network diagram.
[06:52] Maya Chen: great. thanks all. we'll follow up with notes and next steps.

End of call.

Notes on transcription: some speaker overlaps; occasional mis-heard technical terms (KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash), filler words, and slight proper noun errors.

References & attachments mentioned: "commitment & pricing worksheet" (to be attached), "security pack (SOC2 + KMS config guide)", bench harness link (redwood.ai/bench/<redacted>)
